case_studies.title: Autonomy and Agency in Agentic AI: Architectural Tactics for Regulated Contexts
case_studies.abstract: Deploying agentic AI in regulated contexts requires principled reasoning about two design dimensions: agency (what the system can do) and autonomy (how much it acts without human involvement). Though often treated independently, they are coupled: at higher autonomy, human error correction is less available, so reliable operation requires constraining agency accordingly; compliance requirements reinforce this by mandating human involvement as action consequences grow. Yet no established approach addresses them jointly, leaving practitioners without a principled basis for reasoning about oversig
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of balancing autonomy and agency in AI systems, particularly in regulated contexts, by providing architectural tactics to ensure reliable operation and compliance. The authors built a framework to jointly address autonomy and agency, enabling principled reasoning about AI system design. The result provides a basis for designing AI systems that meet regulatory requirements while minimizing human error.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI-powered systems in regulated contexts, here is what to do: review your current AI system design to ensure autonomy and agency are balanced, assess compliance requirements to determine the necessary level of human involvement, and apply the proposed architectural tactics to ensure reliable operation and minimize human error.

case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses agentic AI, which is relevant to IT engineers using JumpCloud, Okta, and other systems that may interact with agentic systems. case_studies.title: No Action Without a NOD: A Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Architecture for Reliable Service Agents
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have increasingly advanced service applications, such as booking flight tickets. However, these service agents suffer from unreliability in long-horizon tasks, as they often produce policy violations, tool hallucinations, and misaligned actions, which greatly impedes their real-world deployment. To address these challenges, we propose NOD (Navigator-Operator-Director), a heterogeneous multi-agent architecture for service agents. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of unreliable service agents in large language models by introducing a new architecture called NOD, which aims to improve the reliability of these agents in long-horizon tasks. The result is a more structured approach to managing task state, reducing errors and misaligned actions. The research focuses on improving language model agents and may not directly impact cloud infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: Covering Human Action Space for Computer Use: Data Synthesis and Benchmark
case_studies.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) automate on-screen work, as illustrated by GPT-5.4 and Claude. Yet their reliability on complex, low-frequency interactions is still poor, limiting user trust. Our analysis of failure cases from advanced models suggests a long-tail pattern in GUI operations, where a relatively small fraction of complex and diverse interactions accounts for a disproportionate share of task failures. case_studies.summary: This research aims to improve the reliability of computer-use agents by creating a benchmark to evaluate their ability to handle complex interactions. The team built a new benchmark called CUActSpot to test models' capabilities. The result is a better understanding of how to improve automated on-screen work, but it's not directly relevant to IT infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: Learning, Fast and Slow: Towards LLMs That Adapt Continually
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained for downstream tasks by updating their parameters (e.g., via RL). However, updating parameters forces them to absorb task-specific information, which can result in catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity. In contrast, in-context learning with fixed LLM parameters can cheaply and rapidly adapt to task-specific requirements (e.g., prompt optimization), but cannot by itself typically match the performance gains available through updating LLM parameters. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models forgetting previous knowledge when updated for new tasks, by creating a system that can adapt continually without losing performance. The authors built a model that combines in-context and in-weights learning to achieve this. The result is a more efficient and effective way of training language models.

case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses LLM adaptation, which is relevant to LLM deployment in IT infrastructure. The concepts might be useful for IT engineers working with LLM APIs. case_studies.title: Predicting Decisions of AI Agents from Limited Interaction through Text-Tabular Modeling
case_studies.abstract: AI agents negotiate and transact in natural language with unfamiliar counterparts: a buyer bot facing an unknown seller, or a procurement assistant negotiating with a supplier. In such interactions, the counterpart's LLM, prompts, control logic, and rule-based fallbacks are hidden, while each decision can have monetary consequences. We ask whether an agent can predict an unfamiliar counterpart's next decision from a few interactions. case_studies.summary: This research aims to predict decisions of AI agents from limited interaction, which can help improve negotiation and transaction outcomes. The authors built a text-tabular model to study this problem in controlled bargaining and negotiation games. The result shows that an agent can predict an unfamiliar counterpart's next decision from a few interactions.

case_studies.title: When Simulation Lies: A Sim-to-Real Benchmark and Domain-Randomized RL Recipe for Tool-Use Agents
case_studies.abstract: Tool-use language agents are evaluated on benchmarks that assume clean inputs, unambiguous tool registries, and reliable APIs. Real deployments violate all these assumptions: user typos propagate into hallucinated tool names, a misconfigured request timeout can stall an agent indefinitely, and duplicate tool names across servers can freeze an SDK. The research focuses on narrowing the gap between simulated and real-world environments, it doesn't directly impact cloud infrastructure management. The study is mainly relevant to the development of language agents and their deployment in various environments.

case_studies.title: Question Difficulty Estimation for Large Language Models via Answer Plausibility Scoring
case_studies.abstract: Estimating question difficulty is a critical component in evaluating and improving large language models (LLMs) for question answering (QA). Existing approaches often rely on readability formulas, retrieval-based signals, or popularity statistics, which may not fully capture the reasoning challenges posed to modern LLMs. In this paper, we introduce Q-DAPS (Question Difficulty based on Answer Plausibility Scores) method, a novel approach that estimates question difficulty by computing the entropy of plausibility scores over candidate answers. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of estimating question difficulty for large language models by introducing a new approach called Q-DAPS, which computes the entropy of plausibility scores over candidate answers, resulting in a more accurate evaluation of language models. The researchers built the Q-DAPS method and tested it across four prominent datasets. This research is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: ORBIT: Preserving Foundational Language Capabilities in GenRetrieval via Origin-Regulated Merging
case_studies.abstract: Despite the rapid advancements in large language model (LLM) development, fine-tuning them for specific tasks often results in the catastrophic forgetting of their general, language-based reasoning abilities. This work investigates and addresses this challenge in the context of the Generative Retrieval (GenRetrieval) task. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models forgetting their general language abilities when fine-tuned for specific tasks, by building a novel approach called ORBIT that preserves these abilities, resulting in improved model performance. ORBIT actively tracks the distance between fine-tuned and original model parameters to prevent this forgetting. This research is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: LychSim: A Controllable and Interactive Simulation Framework for Vision Research
case_studies.abstract: While self-supervised pretraining has reduced vision systems' reliance on synthetic data, simulation remains an indispensable tool for closed-loop optimization and rigorous out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation. However, modern simulation platforms often present steep technical barriers, requiring extensive expertise in computer graphics and game development. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of steep technical barriers in simulation platforms for vision research by building LychSim, a controllable and interactive simulation framework, which resulted in a more accessible tool for closed-loop optimization and out-of-distribution evaluation. LychSim was built using Unreal Engine 5 and features a streamlined Python API. The result is a more user-friendly simulation platform for vision research.

case_studies.title: ORCE: Order-Aware Alignment of Verbalized Confidence in Large Language Models
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce answers with high certainty even when they are incorrect, making reliable confidence estimation essential for deployment in real-world scenarios. Verbalized confidence, where models explicitly state their confidence in natural language, provides a flexible and user-facing uncertainty signal that can be applied even when token logits are unavailable. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of unreliable confidence estimation in large language models by building a new system called ORCE, which aligns verbalized confidence with answer accuracy. The result is a more reliable and trustworthy language model. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.

case_studies.title: MEME: Multi-entity & Evolving Memory Evaluation
case_studies.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly operate in persistent environments where they must store, update, and reason over information across many sessions. While prior benchmarks evaluate only single-entity updates, MEME defines six tasks spanning the full space defined by the multi-entity and evolving axes, including three not scored by prior work: Cascade and Absence (dependency reasoning) and Deletion (post-removal state). case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating memory systems for LLM-based agents in persistent environments. The researchers built a benchmark called MEME to test memory systems across multiple tasks. The result shows that current memory systems struggle with dependency reasoning.

case_studies.title: Do Enterprise Systems Need Learned World Models? The Importance of Context to Infer Dynamics
case_studies.abstract: World models enable agents to anticipate the effects of their actions by internalizing environment dynamics. In enterprise systems, however, these dynamics are often defined by tenant-specific business logic that varies across deployments and evolves over time, making models trained on historical transitions brittle under deployment shift. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of enterprise systems needing to adapt to changing business logic by building a system that can read and apply rules at inference time, resulting in more flexible and robust models. The researchers built a system that can read and apply rules at inference time, rather than relying on learned models. This allows the system to adapt to changing business logic without requiring retraining.

case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper explores how world models affect enterprise systems. While the concept is interesting, its direct applicability to the reader's daily work as an IT engineer is limited.

case_studies.title: Task-Adaptive Embedding Refinement via Test-time LLM Guidance
case_studies.abstract: We explore the effectiveness of an LLM-guided query refinement paradigm for extending the usability of embedding models to challenging zero-shot search and classification tasks. Our approach refines the embedding representation of a user query using feedback from a generative LLM on a small set of documents, enabling embeddings to adapt in real time to the target task. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of improving the accuracy of search and classification tasks by refining embedding models in real-time. The authors built an LLM-guided query refinement approach that adapts to target tasks. The result is a consistent improvement in search and classification benchmarks.

case_studies.title: Stories in Space: In-Context Learning Trajectories in Conceptual Belief Space
case_studies.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) update their behavior in context, which can be viewed as a form of Bayesian inference. However, the structure of the latent hypothesis space over which this inference operates remains unclear. In this work, we propose that LLMs assign beliefs over a low-dimensional geometric space - a conceptual belief space - and that in-context learning corresponds to a trajectory through this space as beliefs are updated over time. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of understanding how Large Language Models update their behavior in context, by proposing that they use a low-dimensional geometric space called a conceptual belief space. The authors built a model to study how beliefs are updated over time in this space. The result is a new way to understand how language models learn and update their understanding of stories and concepts.
